our_denominator: 15 top-engagement 'Black infertility' article links tabulated in Table 1 (the Results text states 9 links remained in the 2020 window and 8 in the 2021 window, i.e. 17)
their_note: 7/15 is a cross-category sum; the paper does not state that aggregate as a verbatim percentage, so the computed value is not acceptable.
our_flag: borderline; loc: Results, Table 1 (Comparison of engagement by platform with graded accuracy of article links); R8 TENSION, FLAGGED FOR ADJUDICATION: the paper reports no overall percentage of misleading/inaccurate links. The value here is the sum of Table 1's five article-subject strata (misleading or inaccurate 2+3+0+1+1 = 7; totals 5+3+3+2+2 = 15). A strict reading of R8 ('never keep a cross-category sum you computed') would drop this row and leave the paper with no extractable value; I kept it because the strata partition one corpus and the numerator category is printed as a single combined column, and because deleting a row is cheaper than recovering a dropped paper. Second problem: Table 1 accounts for 15 links but the Results text says 17 (9 + 8), so the denominator is internally inconsistent. Two windows collapsed to one row; the paper reports no accuracy split by year. Country left Global: nationality of the links is never stated.

our_denominator: 913 geo-located London COVID-19 vaccine tweets drawn from the 12 most common negative-sentiment topic clusters (of 91,473 collected; 8,189 negative-sentiment)
their_quote: 83 tweets (just under 10% of the initial sample) were identified as tweets that contained misinformation (see Figure 3).
their_note: The text states 83 tweets; using the stated 913-tweet denominator gives 83/913 = 9.09%, not the rounded 9.1.
our_flag: borderline; loc: Results, 'Coding Tweets to Hesitancy Themes', p. 4 (Figure 3); Denominator is 913, not 302: the theme percentages elsewhere in the same paragraph (88 = 29%, 72 = 23%, 10 = 3%) are shares of the 302 codeable tweets, but 83/302 = 27.5% would not be 'just under 10%', whereas 83/913 = 9.1% is, and the authors call 913 'the initial sample'. Value derived per R8 as an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts with the same denominator; the paper itself gives only the vague 'just under 10%'. Denominator is heavily curated and NOT platform-representative: it is restricted to tweets the NLP tool scored negative in sentiment (9% of the corpus) and then to the 12 largest negative topic clusters (~1% of the corpus). The share therefore says nothing about misinformation prevalence among all London vaccine tweets, and the authors' own framing of a 'high proportion' should not be read as a platform-level estimate. borderline=true because the operational criterion is 'not verified from reputable sources', which is looser than falsity and could in principle capture a true but unsourced claim; the label is nonetheless explicitly a false-content judgment against an external standard, so the row is coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY, with breadth set to the loosest category.

our_denominator: 487,141 English-language Twitter users assigned a stance (280,713 pro-use + 206,428 anti-use), i.e. the 69.7% of the 698,484 unique users in the English Ivermectin retweet corpus that the propagation reached

Denominator is a single-issue keyword corpus (Ivermectin), so denom_scope = topical and the value is not a general-population sharing rate. The exact denominator for the accuracy domain alone (40 responses x 5 raters) is not printed in the paper; only '400 assessments for each chatbot' across all 8 domains is stated, so the denominator field describes the rating structure rather than quoting a number.
